title: Who Gets to Speak?
focus: 邀请参与并尊重不同表达方式
story:
Priya's first attempt to speak disappears under Daniel's introduction. Her second is covered by the soft electronic sound that announces another person joining the call. By the third, she has stopped raising her hand.

There are seven of us on screen. Four are sitting together in Shanghai, which means that our side conversations reach the microphone as a single busy sound. Priya joins from a small office at the learning centre. A coat hangs behind her. She is still wearing her name badge.

Daniel shares the revised proposal. Elena asks about the proposed group of classes. Rui answers a question about recording changes, and I add something about our tests. Our faces are small squares beside a document that seems to be speaking for us.

Priya opens her mouth. Daniel moves to the next page.

“Sorry,” I say, louder than I intend. “Before we leave that point, Priya had her hand up.”

My own face feels hot. Interrupting the person who runs the meeting still seems more dangerous than losing information. Yet we have arranged this call because Priya knows something we do not.

“Oh, yes.” Daniel stops scrolling. “Go ahead.”

There is a pause while Priya finds the microphone button.

“The afternoon staff don't all have individual email accounts,” she says. “If the invitation to the system goes to an individual account, how will they get in?”

Rui starts to answer, then stops. The proposed access arrangements assume named staff accounts. Sharing a password would hide who changed a class time, but issuing accounts also requires administrative work. Nobody has included that work in the schedule.

“That's a useful catch,” he says. “We need to arrange access before training, not during it.”

“I also have a question about training,” Priya says.

Daniel checks the agenda. I can see him deciding whether to move it to the end. I know what the end of our meetings often looks like: apologies, closing laptops, questions promised another room.

“Could we spend five minutes on the staff steps now?” I ask. “They affect whether the rest of the plan is possible.”

Daniel looks at Elena, who nods. He puts a five-minute timer beside his notes.

Priya explains that a training session at nine would exclude the afternoon team. Recording it might help, but somebody would still need to answer questions. Several staff members work short shifts. Asking them to practise outside paid hours is not a realistic plan.

I begin writing a solution in the chat, then delete it. “What would work with the shifts you already have?”

“Two short sessions,” she says. “And a written page beside the desk. Something we can follow when there's a queue.”

From our side of the table, an analyst named Noor raises a finger. She has been checking the draft instructions. When she speaks, Rui answers before she reaches the end of her sentence.

“I know,” he says. “We can simplify the screen.”

“That isn't quite what I mean.”

Rui turns back towards her. “Sorry. Finish.”

Noor points to the instructions. “They tell staff what to do when everything succeeds. They don't tell staff when to stop.”

I write that sentence down exactly.

Priya gives a brief, tired laugh. “Yes. That's the page I'd like.”

We use the rest of the five minutes to identify stopping points. If staff cannot confirm the correct class, they do not guess. If a saved change does not appear, they do not repeatedly press the same button. They use the agreed fallback and record what happened for the team to check. These are proposed instructions; we still need to test them with the centre.

When the timer rings, Daniel lets the final sentence finish. Then he says, “We need another ten minutes for decisions. Does anyone have to leave at the original time?”

Priya does. The reception desk needs her back.

We rearrange the remaining items so that she can answer the questions only she can answer. The technical discussion continues after she leaves. Before going, she offers to review the draft page on Thursday, between shifts, if we send it in advance.

Later, I ask Noor whether she wants me to invite her in earlier next time.

“Sometimes,” she says. “But don't assume I'm waiting to be rescued. I was reading the document for most of that meeting.”

“I thought you couldn't find a gap.”

“For that point, I couldn't. For the others, I didn't have anything to add.”

It is a small distinction, and an important one. I thank her for saying it. She suggests putting questions in the agenda beforehand so people can prepare a response or leave a written comment.

A message comes from Priya while Noor and I are still talking. She has found cover for the first short training session. For the second she can have Elena herself on reception, provided we finish before a tutor brings down the afternoon register.

I read the message aloud. Daniel says, “Good. So training is sorted.”

A second message arrives. Priya types fast when she can get both hands free. It says: Please ask Elena whether she's used the new desk phone.

Daniel stops with his fingers above the keys. “Is she joking?”

Nobody knows. He asks. Elena sends back a picture of the phone. A yellow slip over one button reads TRANSFER. Another, with an arrow pointing the other way, reads REALLY TRANSFER.

Noor starts laughing and has to take off her glasses. Five minutes later Elena confirms she'll come down early and practise taking a call before Priya leaves the desk. We move the invitation back to give her those five minutes.

I send Priya the new times. Her reply is one word: Lovely. A little later she adds: Especially the bit where I actually get to leave.

phrases.zh: 暂缓换题并引回遗漏内容

phrases.en: That isn’t quite what I mean.
Does anyone have to leave at the original time?
You can also leave a written comment.
I didn’t have anything to add.
phrases.zh: 说明沉默并不等于被排除

practice.grammar: 练习过去完成时交代先前发生的事：Priya had stopped raising her hand before Andy invited her to speak. 用同样结构描述她先尝试发言、随后放弃的顺序。
practice.pronunciation: 读 That isn’t quite / what I mean. 先轻读 quite，重读 mean；再重读 quite，体会保留、纠正的语气差异，选择较礼貌的一版录音回听。

questions.q: What practical issue does Priya raise first?
questions.a: Some afternoon staff do not have individual email accounts for access invitations.

questions.q: Why does Elena need a few minutes before the training?
questions.a: She will cover reception and needs to practise using its phone.

questions.q: Why does Noor challenge Andy’s assumption?
questions.a: She was sometimes reading or had nothing to add; she did not always need an invitation to speak.

roleplay.context: 你扮演 Andy，主持一个多人远程会议，留出空间但不替别人发言。

turns.line: Let’s move to the next page.
turns.cue: 礼貌打断，指出 Priya 刚才想发言

turns.line: I need to return to the reception desk in ten minutes.
turns.cue: 调整议程优先处理需要她参与的事项

turns.line: I don’t always want someone to call on me.
turns.cue: 承认自己的假设，询问更适合的参与方式

practice.transfer: 组织一次朋友旅行讨论。口头给出开场说明：允许轮流发言、跳过一轮或稍后留言；随后邀请一位安静的朋友，同时明确没有发言压力。
practice.retell: 用两分钟复述会议中的两个不同问题：发言机会被遮盖，以及沉默被误读。用具体人物反应支撑区别。

translations.20-1: Priya第一次想开口，声音淹没在Daniel的开场介绍里。
translations.20-2: 第二次，又被提示有人加入通话的轻柔电子音盖住了。
translations.20-3: 到了第三次，她已经不再举手了。
translations.20-5: 其中四个人一起坐在上海的会议室里，这意味着我们彼此间的小声交谈，传到麦克风里就成了一团嘈杂的声音。
translations.20-6: Priya在学习中心的一间小办公室里参加会议。
translations.20-10: Elena询问了拟定参与试点的课程。
translations.20-11: Rui回答了一个关于记录修改的问题，我又补充了些测试情况。
translations.20-12: 我们的脸缩在文档旁的小方框里，那份文档仿佛正在替我们说话。
translations.20-15: “不好意思。”我说，声音比原本打算的还大。
translations.20-16: “在进入下一项之前，Priya刚才一直举着手。”
translations.20-17: 我自己的脸也开始发烫。
translations.20-18: 打断会议主持人，对我来说似乎仍比漏掉信息更危险。
translations.20-19: 可我们安排这次通话，正是因为Priya知道一些我们不知道的情况。
translations.20-23: Priya找麦克风按钮时，大家等了一会儿。
translations.20-24: “下午班的工作人员并不是每个人都有独立邮箱。”她说。
translations.20-25: “如果系统邀请发到个人账号，他们要怎么登录？”
translations.20-27: 拟定的访问方案默认每位工作人员都有自己的实名账号。
translations.20-28: 共用密码会让人无法分辨是谁修改了课程时间，但分配账号也需要管理工作。
translations.20-29: 没有人把这项工作排进日程。
translations.20-30: “你发现了一个关键问题。”他说。
translations.20-31: “我们得在培训前安排好登录权限，而不是培训时再处理。”
translations.20-34: 我看得出，他在考虑要不要把这个问题放到最后。
translations.20-35: 我知道我们的会议结束时常是什么样：说着抱歉、合上电脑，再承诺把问题留到别的会议里讨论。
translations.20-36: “我们现在能不能先花五分钟，过一下工作人员要做的步骤？”我问。
translations.20-37: “这些步骤会影响计划的其余部分能否执行。”
translations.20-39: 他在笔记旁设置了一个五分钟的计时器。
translations.20-40: Priya解释说，如果培训安排在九点，下午班的团队就没法参加。
translations.20-41: 录下来可能有帮助，但还是需要有人回答问题。
translations.20-42: 有几位工作人员的班次很短。
translations.20-43: 让他们在不计薪的时间里练习，并不是现实的方案。
translations.20-44: 我开始在聊天框里写解决办法，又删掉了。
translations.20-45: “按现有排班，怎样安排比较可行？”
translations.20-47: “另外，在前台放一页书面说明。
translations.20-48: 有人排队的时候，我们也能照着操作。”
translations.20-49: 坐在我们这一侧的一位分析师Noor举起了一根手指。
translations.20-50: 她一直在检查操作说明草稿。
translations.20-51: 她刚开口，还没说完，Rui就接上了话。
translations.20-59: “这里告诉工作人员一切顺利时该怎么做。
translations.20-60: 却没告诉他们什么时候该停下来。”
translations.20-61: 我一字不差地记下了这句话。
translations.20-64: 这才是我想要的那页说明。”
translations.20-65: 剩下的几分钟里，我们一起列出需要停止操作的情况。
translations.20-66: 如果工作人员无法确认是不是正确的课程，就不要猜。
translations.20-67: 如果保存后的修改没有显示出来，就不要反复按同一个按钮。
translations.20-68: 他们应该使用约定的备用流程，并记录发生的情况，供团队检查。
translations.20-69: 这些只是拟定的说明，我们还需要和中心一起验证。
translations.20-70: 计时器响起时，Daniel让正在说话的人把最后一句说完。
translations.20-71: 接着他说：“我们还需要十分钟作决定。
translations.20-72: 有人必须按原定时间离开吗？”
translations.20-75: 我们重新安排了剩下的事项，让她先回答只有她能回答的问题。
translations.20-76: 她离开后，技术讨论继续进行。
translations.20-77: 临走前她表示，如果我们提前发过去，她可以在周四换班间隙看一遍那页说明草稿。
translations.20-78: 后来，我问Noor，下次她是否希望我早点请她发言。
translations.20-80: “但别以为我一直在等人救场。
translations.20-81: 那场会议的大部分时间，我都在读文档。”
translations.20-82: “我以为你一直找不到机会插话。”
translations.20-84: 其他地方，我没有什么要补充的。”
translations.20-85: 这是个细微却重要的区别。
translations.20-87: 她建议提前把问题放进议程，让大家可以准备回答，或者留下书面意见。
translations.20-88: 我和Noor还在说话，Priya就发来了消息。
translations.20-89: 第一场短时培训，她已经找好了顶班的人。
translations.20-90: 第二场可以让Elena亲自守前台，前提是我们得在老师把下午的点名册送下来之前结束。
translations.20-95: Priya只要能腾出两只手，打字就飞快。
translations.20-96: 上面写着：麻烦问问Elena，她用过前台的新电话没有。
translations.20-97: Daniel停了下来，手指悬在键盘上方。
translations.20-101: Elena发回来一张电话的照片。
translations.20-102: 一个按键上方贴着张黄色纸条，写着“转接”。
translations.20-103: 另一张的箭头指向相反的方向，写的是“真要转接按这个”。
translations.20-104: Noor笑得只好把眼镜摘下来。
translations.20-105: 五分钟后，Elena确认她会早点下来，趁Priya还在前台先练习接个电话。
translations.20-106: 我们把邀请上的时间往后挪，给她留出这五分钟。
translations.20-108: 她只回了一个词：太好了。
translations.20-109: 过了一小会儿，她又补了一句：尤其好的是，这回我真能离开前台了。
